/hr/ghcr.io-bjw-s-labs-charts-immich-mic.doc:
Immich is a self-hosted photo and video backup solution.

For immich, there are multiple helm deployments:

  • immich-web
  • immich-server
  • immich-typesense
  • immich-machine-learning
  • immich-microservices (this one)

For redis and postgres, there are multiple helm charts:

  • Redis: app-template/redis, bitnami/redis
  • PostgreSQL: operator cloudnative-pg/cloudnative-pg, bitnami bitnami/postgresql

/hr/ghcr.io-home-operations-charts-mirro.title: external-dns helm release
/hr/ghcr.io-home-operations-charts-mirro.name: external-dns
/hr/ghcr.io-home-operations-charts-mirro.doc: ExternalDNS is a Kubernetes add-on that automatically manages the creation and updates of DNS records for services running in your cluster. It integrates with a variety of DNS providers, such as CloudFlare DNS, Amazon Route 53, Google Cloud DNS, and more, to ensure that your applications are easily accessible from anywhere with a DNS name. With ExternalDNS, you can simplify the process of managing DNS records for your home lab, eliminating the need for manual updates and reducing the risk of errors.

0:
upstreams:
  init:
    # answer queries immediately instead of blocking on upstream checks
    strategy: fast
  groups:
    default:
      - tcp-tls:one.one.one.one:853
      - tcp-tls:dns.quad9.net:853
  strategy: parallel_best
  timeout: 2s

# resolves the DoT hostnames above, avoiding a chicken-and-egg at startup
bootstrapDns:
  - tcp+udp:1.1.1.1
  - tcp+udp:9.9.9.9

# static records for hosts outside the cluster. Resolved above the
# conditional forward below, so these win; every other name under
# the domain still falls through to k8s-gateway.
# customDNS:
#   mapping:
#     analytics.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     auth.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     budget.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     budget-tap.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     budget-tap-pz.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     dash.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     feed.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     forge.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     idp-home.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     pf.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     portfolio-staging.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     prx-home.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     pz8-home.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     sure.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     whoami-home.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.11
#     pve1.lan.${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.1.3

conditional:
  # a miss stays a miss, never leaks the internal name to Cloudflare
  fallbackUpstream: false
  mapping:
    ${SECRET_DOMAIN}: 192.168.100.103

blocking:
  denylists:
    main:
      - https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/hagezi/dns-blocklists@latest/wildcard/pro.txt
      - https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/hagezi/dns-blocklists@latest/wildcard/tif.txt
      - https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/hagezi/dns-blocklists@latest/wildcard/fake.txt
  allowlists:
    main: []
  clientGroupsBlock:
    default:
      - main
  blockType: zeroIp
  loading:
    # 24h, not 4h. Each replica re-downloads every list in full on
    # every refresh -- there is no conditional GET and no sharing
    # between replicas -- and these lists are large:
    #   tif.txt   52.6 MB
    #   pro.txt    4.8 MB
    #   fake.txt   0.3 MB
    # 57.7 MB per replica, three replicas, so 173 MB per cycle. At
    # 4h that was ~1.04 GB/day in six bursts, and on a ~51 Mbit DSL
    # each burst is roughly 27 seconds of fully saturated downlink.
    # All three refresh within about two minutes of each other, so
    # they stack rather than spread.
    #
    # That is a latency event, not a bandwidth cost: with
    # bufferbloat on the line, 27 seconds of saturation is 27
    # seconds of unusable interactive traffic. Six a day.
    #
    # The lists change on the order of days, so 4h bought nothing.
    # Note the period runs from pod start, not wall clock, so the
    # burst drifts -- it cannot be pinned to the small hours.
    refreshPeriod: 24h
    # serve while lists are still downloading
    strategy: fast
    downloads:
      # the wildcard lists are large, 60s is not enough
      timeout: 4m
      attempts: 3
      cooldown: 10s

caching:
  minTime: 5m
  maxTime: 30m
  # Both of these default to 0, which means unlimited, and that is
  # what was killing this pod: the denylists below are already
  # several hundred MB resident (tif.txt alone is 52MB of text),
  # so an unbounded cache on top of them reached the memory limit
  # and each replica was OOMKilled roughly four times a day.
  # Soft limits, so entries are evicted rather than queries failed.
  maxItemsCount: 25000
  prefetching: true
  prefetchMaxItemsCount: 2000

# Shared cache across the three replicas. Without this each one
# keeps its own, so a client that the LoadBalancer sends to a
# different replica than last time misses and pays a full upstream
# round trip -- with three replicas roughly two thirds of the
# warm answers were unreachable to any given query.
#
# Reads stay in-process: the Redis layer is a decorator over the
# local cache that replicates entries over a pub/sub channel, so
# nothing is added to the resolve path. Writes go through a bounded
# send buffer that drops rather than blocks, which is why a slow or
# full cache cannot stall a query.
#
# required is false on purpose, and it is the default: Dragonfly
# being down has to degrade to local caching, never stop DNS. The
# whole house resolves through here, including the tailnet.
redis:
  address: blocky-dragonfly:6379
  required: false

prometheus:
  enable: true
  path: /metrics

ports:
  dns:
    - 5353
  http:
    - 4000

queryLog:
  type: console

log:
  level: info
  format: json
